analysis.title: Trump's scorecard ahead of the midterms
key_insights: Syz's CIO team scores Trump's second term 21 months in: pledges that depended on executive action or a single reconciliation bill (border, taxes, regulation) were largely delivered, while pledges that depended on markets, the Fed or foreign adversaries (prices, rates, peace) mostly were not.

Polling ahead of the 3 November midterms is weak for the President: a Washington Post-ABC-Ipsos poll (9-13 October) has approval at 33%, the lowest of the term, with 28% approving of his handling of the economy and Democrats up 8 points on the generic congressional ballot. An AP-NORC poll has 17% approving of his management of the cost of living.

Border: Border Patrol recorded 98,708 southwest border apprehensions in fiscal 2026, about 95% below the Biden-era annual average and the lowest since the late 1960s. Nationwide encounters of 379,243 were the lowest on record. About 250 miles of new barrier has been built since January 2025.

Taxes: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act made the 2017 individual tax cuts permanent and added relief on tips, overtime and seniors. CBO estimates it adds USD 4.7tn to deficits through 2035 including interest and macro effects, and projects the fiscal 2026 deficit at USD 1.9tn, or 5.8% of GDP.

Deregulation went further than promised: OMB counted 218 deregulatory actions against five significant new rules in fiscal 2025. The US left the Paris Agreement again, the EPA rescinded the endangerment finding, and much of the IRA clean-energy credit structure was scaled back.

Energy: US crude output is forecast at 13.9m barrels a day in 2026 and marketed natural gas at a record 122.5 bcf/d (EIA). LNG exports are expected to average 17.6 bcf/d in 2026, nearly 50% above 2024. Crude growth has slowed, and shale was already at records before this administration.

Inflation: September CPI rose 0.6% m/m and 3.7% y/y (BLS), up from 2.9% when Biden left office. Gasoline rose 9.1% in the month and accounted for more than half of the headline rise. Core CPI rose 0.3% m/m, above expectations, so price pressure extends beyond oil.

The Iran conflict, begun in late February, and the near-closure of the Strait of Hormuz caused the largest oil supply shock on record. Brent hit an intraday high of $126.41 on 30 April and is back above $110. September pump prices averaged $4.33 a gallon, a record for the month. The Strategic Petroleum Reserve is at its lowest since the early 1980s.

Rates: the Fed raised its policy rate in September to 3.75-4.00%, its first hike in more than three years. The 30-year mortgage rate averaged 7.4% in mid-October (Freddie Mac), higher than in January 2025. Long-dated Treasury yields have risen with inflation and deficit concerns.

Trade: the goods and services deficit widened to USD 105.6bn in August (BEA). The Supreme Court ruled 6-3 in February that IEEPA does not authorise tariffs, striking down the reciprocal and fentanyl duties and opening the door to refunds. The White House moved to a temporary Section 122 global surcharge and Section 232 and 301 sector duties, which rest on narrower legal footing.

Growth and labour: Q2 GDP grew at a 2.2% annualised rate (BEA), the Atlanta Fed nowcast points to faster Q3 growth, and the main engine is AI capital spending. September payrolls rose only 29,000 and unemployment edged up to 4.2%.

Equities: the S&P 500 set a record close of 7,818.93 on 6 October and is up about 14% this year. AI-linked companies are close to half of index market cap and drove around two-thirds of the year's rise.

Market implications: inflation is now the binding constraint and rapid rate cuts have receded. Permanent tax cuts, lower tariff revenue after the court ruling and war costs point to wider deficits and more Treasury issuance, which tends to push long-dated yields up. A Democratic House would likely freeze policy rather than reverse it, with tax law unchanged and trade, immigration and regulation staying under presidential control.

Unresolved wars: the Ukraine war is in its fifth year with trilateral talks unscheduled and the Kremlin demanding Donbas territory. The Iran conflict is approaching its eighth month, and the Pentagon puts its cost above USD 40bn.

tension_points.bull_case: Supporters argue the Iran war and the AI-driven power crunch were shocks no president could have avoided, and that the border and tax record will pay off over time.
tension_points.bear_case: Critics argue the war and the tariffs were deliberate choices whose burden fell on the voters who had been promised relief.

tension_points.bull_case: A divided Congress would be more likely to freeze policy than reverse it, leaving tax law unchanged and trade, immigration and regulation under presidential control.
tension_points.bear_case: A Democratic House, as polls suggest, would intensify oversight and budget battles, and the Fed tightening with headline CPI near 4% limits rate cuts.
